earlier_scan.source_named: Houis, Maurice. 1963. Etude descriptive de la langue Susu (standard grammar, incl. prosody; not online). Brunton 1802 grammar (archive.org, read) marks only vowel length 'accents', no stress-placement statement; Peace Corps Susu manual (read) has none

new_statements.quote: In words of two syllables the accent is usually placed on the first syllable : as "male" ("rice") = "ma-le"; "bende" ("dirt") = "ben-de"; "kubbe" ("ashes" or "dust") = "kub-be"; "heri" ("peace") = "he-ri." In words of three syllables, if they are simple words, the accent is on the antepenult: as "harrige" ("lot" or "portion"); "yammine" ("a kingdom"); "bellaxe" ("a hand"); "wellaxe" ("a wooden slate"). In compound words the accent retains the place it has in the simple words.
new_statements.citation: Douglin, Philip Henry. 1887. A reading book in the Soso language. London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge.
new_statements.locator: Introduction (intended for the teacher), section 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7 (PDF pp. 18-19 of the archive.org scan readingbookinsos00dougiala)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the first syllable: on the initial syllable of disyllables ('usually') and on the antepenult, i.e. the first syllable, of simple trisyllables; compounds keep the accent of each simple member (so a compound has more than one accent).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; compounds retain the accent of each simple constituent.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'usually' for disyllables; only simple (non-compound) trisyllables are covered; no data on longer words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (reading pronunciation of isolated words in a teacher's introduction). Modern descriptions (Sangster & Faber 1968; Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013) treat Susu as a tone language with H/L melodies and say nothing about stress; Douglin's 'accent' is a 19th-century missionary's impression and may reflect the H-initial tonal melodies rather than a stress accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Douglin 1887 describes the Susu of the Rio Pongo (Guinea) / Sierra Leone SPG mission area ('Soso-land'); he notes only one dialect difference (Moria s > sh). Glottolog lists susu1250 without dialect subdivisions, so the statement is for the language as a whole; the 19th-century 'accent' should be read against the modern tonal analyses (Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013; Sangster & Faber 1968), which describe Susu as a two-tone language and are silent on stress.

sources.note: Introduction 'ACCENT' (pp. 6-7; PDF pp. 18-19): in disyllables the accent is usually on the first syllable (ma-le 'rice', ben-de 'dirt', kub-be 'ashes', he-ri 'peace'); in simple trisyllables on the antepenult (harrige, yammine, bellaxe, wellaxe); compounds keep the accent of the simple words. No mention of tone.

sources.note: 'Of the Letters' / 'Of Pronunciation': the acute accent marks short vowels only ('the voice to dwell shorter time on it'); no statement of stress placement.

sources.citation: Green, Christopher R., Jonathan C. Anderson & Samuel G. Obeng. 2013. Interacting tonal processes in Susu. Mandenkan 50: 61-84. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.876
sources.note: Tonal analysis only: mono-/disyllabic nouns carry H, HL or LH melodies; TBU is the mora (citing Vydrine 2002); feet are invoked for tone neutralization; no statement about stress or accent in Susu (foot-head 'prominence' is mentioned only in a footnote about Bambara).

sources.citation: Sangster, Linda W. & Emmanuel Faber. 1969. Susu Intermediate Course. Final Report. Bloomington: Indiana University (ERIC ED 029 297), 246 pp.
sources.note: No phonology section; only incidental references to tone on the last vowel of derived nouns; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Sangster, Linda & Emmanuel Faber. 1968. Susu Basic Course. Final Report. Bloomington: Indiana University (ERIC ED 029 296; NDEA-6-602), 488 pp.
sources.note: Pre-speech units 'Intonation' and 'Tones': Susu has tones on each vowel (neutral/mid, high, low, high-falling, low-rising) with sentence intonation superimposed; derived nouns are distinguished 'by the tone on the last syllable' (French text: 'l'accentuation sur la dernière syllabe'); no word-stress rule stated. (scanned text of the ERIC fiche; 112 MB PDF not downloaded.)
